#5314. Binance’s $6.3B Hack Fix Is Coming Tomorrow: Why the ZK Math Doesn't Tell the Whole Story

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

On-chain data shows the attacker behind the $6.3 billion Binance theft depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses.

At the same time, Binance's first post-hack reserve snapshot shows its biggest assets covered with buffers as small as 2.7 ETH and $6 of USDT. Binance's full zero-knowledge proof of those figures is due by Tuesday.

Some of the money stolen from Binance has started going back to Binance.

Blockchain intelligence firm Arkham has flagged the entity it tracks as "Binance Hacker" depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses. Arkham says those addresses "likely represent nested service(s)." These are third-party exchanges that use Binance for liquidity and custody, giving their own customers deposit addresses that sit on Binance's infrastructure.

If Arkham is right, the hacker isn't depositing into an ordinary Binance account. The money would be going to smaller platforms that operate through Binance. Exchanges have long known this is a weak point for stolen funds moving into normal trading. Either way, Binance is now receiving stolen funds at its own deposit addresses while it works to show customers it has replaced what was taken.

The FBI has attributed the October 29 theft to North Korea. The deposits come at a sensitive moment. Binance has just published its first reserve snapshot since the hack and has promised a full cryptographic proof of it by Tuesday.

$4 million is a small slice of a theft worth about $6.3 billion, but it matters for two reasons.

It shows how the laundering works. Nested services are a common way into the regulated financial system. A third-party platform that relies on Binance for custody may run weaker identity checks on its own users. Funds deposited there can be swapped and withdrawn without the hacker ever opening a Binance account.

Binance can act on it. Binance can't freeze bitcoin and ether sitting in wallets nobody controls, and it doesn't control the stablecoins that issuers like Tether and Circle have frozen. Deposits that land at its own addresses are different: they are on Binance's platform, so Binance can freeze them itself. One of the first tests of how Binance handles the money still in the hacker's hands is whether it freezes these funds and identifies the services that own the addresses.

While the hacker's funds move, Binance has been rebuilding its reserves. Its proof-of-reserves page now shows:

The first page covers Binance's six largest assets. Customer balances are what users hold. Reserves are on-chain wallet balances, including assets held with outside custodians.

The second page has four more assets, and two of them stand out:

Why USD1 and RLUSD matter: these are two of the stablecoins whose issuers froze stolen funds after the attack. World Liberty Financial froze $27 million of USD1, and Ripple began freezing RLUSD the same night. Both now show reserves above what Binance owes customers.

Assets with outside custodians: part of several reserves sits with outside custodians rather than in Binance's own exchange wallets:

The striking part isn't that the ratios reach 100%. It's how closely they stop there.

Compared with October's report: Binance's previous monthly report, published in early October before the hack, showed BTC at 100.35% and USDT at 103.88%. ETH was already at exactly 100.00%. After the theft:

Not every asset is that tight. USDC, ZEC and BNB carry buffers of 1.3% to 6%. The thinnest buffers are in BTC, ETH, USDT and SOL, which are among the assets the attacker took in the largest amounts.

How Binance says it got here: the pattern fits Binance's account of replacing the stolen assets in stages. It reported 80% replaced on Friday, 90% on Saturday and 95% on Sunday. The remaining 5% is in less-liquid tokens it is still buying. The money came from:

Binance confirmed taking 7,499 BTC from SAFU and has pledged to refill the fund to about $1 billion.

What the snapshot can't show: it was taken a little over a day after the theft, once the rebuild was under way. It shows the balance sheet after the replacement, not how large the gap was on October 29.

Binance says the full proof takes 40 to 50 hours to compute. Its latest update says it will be ready "by Tuesday, 2026-11-03 (UTC)." The system is open source, in Binance's zkmerkle-proof-of-solvency repository.

What the proof guarantees, according to the project's circuit design document:

The design also guards against a "dummy user attack" identified by Ethereum Foundation researcher Enrico Bottazzi. In that attack, fake accounts holding cheap tokens are used to offset debts in major assets.

What it doesn't prove: the reserve side. The project's verifier config describes the totals as information "published by CEX, it represents CEX's liability." The reserve figures are checked a different way, against the wallet addresses Binance publishes through the page's "Download All Address" option.

What customers can do: each user can get a Merkle proof for their account and check it against the published root. They can use the verifier code in Binance's repository rather than Binance's own interface. That doesn't prove Binance is solvent, but it confirms the user's balance was counted.

Binance has rebuilt its reserves to 100% across its ten largest assets, but on several of them the buffer is only a few coins. Meanwhile, stolen funds are reaching its deposit addresses through platforms that run on its infrastructure. Tuesday's proof can confirm customer balances. It can't show how Binance handles the stolen money arriving at its own door.

#5313. Zcash’s Game-Changing NU7 Upgrade Goes Live, Slashing Block Times 3X as $5,000 ZEC Rally Comes Into Focus

NU7 has successfully activated on mainnet. A new era of Zcash is here. $ZEC pic.twitter.com/rPaSFe9h7j

The Network Sustainability Mechanism addresses a long-term challenge that Zcash shares with Bitcoin: how to keep its network secure as mining rewards decline with each halving. As block subsidies become smaller, both networks face questions about whether transaction fees alone can provide enough incentive for miners to continue securing the blockchain.

Under the new mechanism, 60% of transaction fees from each block goes into a publicly visible reserve, while miners receive the remaining 40%. The approach creates a dedicated funding pool to support Zcash’s long-term security and sustainability while preserving its hard-capped supply of 21 million ZEC.

The reserved fees are scheduled to be gradually reissued through block rewards starting at block 8,939,664, expected in 2031, with the recycled funds distributed along a smooth curve on top of the existing halving schedule.

NU7 also introduces a cap on the amount of shielded transaction activity that can be included in each block, reducing the volume of data wallets need to scan when searching for incoming payments. This is expected to make wallet synchronization more efficient and improve the overall user experience.

Despite the major network upgrade, ZEC has yet to register a strong bullish market reaction. The cryptocurrency was down 0.8% over the past 24 hours, trading at $1,313 at press time, as broader weakness across the crypto market weighed on prices.

Despite the recent price pullback, some prominent crypto investors remain bullish on Zcash’s longer-term prospects. Chris Burniske, a renowned investor known for his early interest in Solana (SOL), pointed to the ZEC/BTC chart as the key indicator to watch, describing it as “still the only chart that matters as it shows what comes next.”

#5311. Binance Says Its $6.3 Billion Hack Began With a Fake Job Interview, but Traders Aren’t Convinced

Binance said on Tuesday, November 3, that the Binance hack started with a fake job interview, in which North Korean hackers gave one of its engineers a coding test laced with malware, but many traders still doubt that is the whole story.

The October 29 theft took $6.34 billion from Binance’s hot wallets, the largest crypto heist on record. Binance’s incident report describes a campaign that ran for months: a tampered download in June, the fake interview in September and an internal AI tool that led the attackers to the engineers who ran its wallets.

Not everyone is buying it. Since the hack, traders on X have called it an inside job. They point to how fast the money left, across ten blockchains in about 20 minutes, and to how often Binance’s account has changed.

BREAKING: Binance says hackers used a fake job interview to infect an employee's computer.The malware let them hijack Binance's internal AI tool, take over more engineers' accounts, and drain $6.34 billion from its hot wallets.

No one has offered proof. The FBI has tied the theft to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group, and blockchain analytics firm TRM Labs agrees with high confidence.

BNB hasn’t recovered either. It trades at $703.33, up 0.7% today but still 7.4% below its $759.85 close the day before the hack.

So what exactly does Binance say happened, and why are traders still unconvinced?

Slowly, through three engineers. Binance co-CEO Richard Teng told CNBC the attackers “spent months building their way in” and rejected the idea that a single laptop was the weak point.

“This wasn’t one mistake or one breach – it was a months-long campaign,” Teng wrote on X.

Binance says users won’t lose anything. It has replaced 98% of the stolen assets with its own funds, and about $2.85 billion has been frozen or intercepted with the help of Tether, Circle and others.

Discover: Bitcoin Settles Its $10.9 Billion Options Expiry Right on Max Pain After the Binance Hack

Because the doubts started before the report, and the report didn’t settle them. Two days after the theft, trader Financelancelot called it “totally an inside job,” and Solana trader Ansem wrote: “My trust in binance is gone.”

The skeptics keep coming back to five points:

The proof of reserves didn’t help. Binance’s November 2 proof used an October 31 snapshot, taken after it had already bought back most of the stolen coins, so critics say it can’t show how big the hole was.

A hack of this scale means serious security failures occurred. No platform is unhackable, but that cannot be an excuse. Every incident exposes weaknesses that should have been prevented.Some details are embarrassing. Public explanations also simplify what appears to have been a… https://t.co/ZMAjZt2hF8

Some of the louder claims have already fallen apart. A viral post blaming a North Korean “honey trap” passed 800,000 views before co-founder Yi He called it untrue and said ZachXBT, the investigator it quoted, never said it.

An employee’s laptop being the way in doesn’t make it an inside job. Fake job offers with booby-trapped coding tests are TraderTraitor’s best-known trick, the same group behind the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in February 2025.

Less than half of it has been stopped. Of the $6.34 billion taken, Binance says $2.85 billion has been frozen or intercepted, much of it stablecoins that Tether and Circle could lock.

The rest is on the move. Blockchain analytics firm Elliptic counts about $3.24 billion still in addresses linked to the attackers, and Chainalysis has found the stolen funds mixed with money from September’s Bitget exploit.

One pile hasn’t moved at all. The 233.46 million XRP taken from Binance, worth about $299 million, has sat in six wallets since November 2, untouched as of Wednesday morning.

Discover: Bitcoin Sellers Take a Week of Losses Below $80,000 as Strategy and Strive Keep Buying: Will $75,000 Hold?

More proof, and soon. Three things are due in the next few days:

Not yet. BNB fell 8.1% on October 29, from $759.85 to $698.46, on $414 million in volume, more than four times what it traded the day before.

It has leaned on its 200-day EMA ever since. BNB dipped to $680.74 earlier today, close to the $680 hack low, and bounced back to $703.33.

Binance has told its version of the Binance hack in detail. Until the independent review backs it up, traders will keep reading BNB’s chart as a vote of confidence.

#5310. 'Don’t Be Silly': Satoshi Associate Dismisses Bitcoin Quantum Collapse Claims

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. Bitcoin developers have renewed the discussion about the long-term security of the network amid the development of quantum computing ("Q-Day"). The trigger was an interview StarkWare CEO Eli Ben-Sasson gave to journalist Pete Rizzo.

According to Ben-Sasson, without the implementation of a "quantum fix," Bitcoin will lose its leadership, and its market value will collapse due to the physical limitations of current computing systems.

Criticism of these forecasts came from Adam Back, the creator of Hashcash, co-founder of Blockstream and one of the cryptographers mentioned by Satoshi Nakamoto in the Bitcoin whitepaper. On the social network X, Back described the panic expectations with the phrase: "c'mon guys, don't be silly and alarmist."

According to Back, the risks are exaggerated, since algorithms for protection against quantum threats are already at the protocol planning stage. He pointed out that Ben-Sasson's own company, StarkWare, builds its products on STARK technology: zero-knowledge proofs that run on cryptographic hash functions.

In the Bitcoin technical community, hash functions are considered the main security factor. According to theoretical models, quantum computers running Shor's algorithm are capable of breaking the network's current asymmetric cryptography (ECDSA and Schnorr).

However, this method is ineffective against hash functions (including SHA-256). Grover's algorithm gives quantum systems only a quadratic speedup in brute-force search, which, according to Back, is fully neutralized by Bitcoin's standard security settings.

As an alternative scenario, Satoshi Nakamoto's associate cited data on the community's current technical developments, which by late 2026 have moved into the testing phase:

SHRINCS protocol: A modified hash-based signature (Shrunken SPHINCS). According to Blockstream developers, they optimized it for Bitcoin's bandwidth limits.

Implementation status: An official draft Bitcoin Improvement Proposal (BIP) has been published for review. According to the project's roadmap, the technology is undergoing stress tests on the Liquid sidechain.

Critics of post-quantum cryptography often name data volume as the main problem. Quantum-resistant signatures are bulkier than standard 64-byte Schnorr keys, which, according to a number of researchers, could overload the blockchain and raise fees.

Back argues that the infrastructure is capable of scaling through data aggregation. According to his position, batch verification methods and STARK hash proofs make it possible to compress thousands of signatures into one compact package. According to supporters of this approach, the solution will preserve the network's speed and protect its decentralization.

The current discussion demonstrates the existence of two polar views: part of the industry considers the quantum threat an urgent problem, while Bitcoin core developers speak of planned testing of the protective infrastructure, which is proceeding in parallel with the development of quantum capabilities.

The incident developed in the context of a public discussion started by influencer JC Rivera , who reproached the XRP community for systematic skepticism toward new startups. In response, opponents led by Kaj Leroy justified the community’s wariness with the new project’s on-chain data.

Reece Merrick, Ripple Senior Executive Officer/Managing Director, Middle East & Africa, attended the recently concluded Dubai Fintech Summit held between November 2 and 3, 2026, organized by DIFC as part of Dubai Future Finance Week.

In 2024, Ripple announced a partnership with the DIFC Innovation Hub, the thriving innovation ecosystem of the Dubai International Financial Centre (DIFC), to accelerate blockchain innovation in the UAE.

Ripple announced in 2026 its expansion in the UAE with the opening of its Middle East and Africa (MEA) regional headquarters in the Dubai International Financial Centre (DIFC). The announcement highlighted the firm's strategic presence in the country.

Markets with "opening hours" simply won't cut it. ➡️ Bridging TradFi & DeFi: Scaling tokenized markets requires real bank-grade infrastructure, custody, and risk management. At @Ripple, we see every day how enterprise rails, tokenization, and stablecoins bridge this gap 🇦🇪

In a recent X post, Merrick highlighted his participation at the Dubai Fintech Summit as part of a panel that explored how digital assets could scale. The details gathered from his X post revealed that representatives from BlackRock, Standard Chartered and Robinhood were also participants in this discussion.

Merrick said the consensus among participants was clear, as the question was no longer whether institutional adoption would happen, but what infrastructure needed to change to support it.

The Ripple executive went on to share a few takeaways from the discussion with BlackRock, Standard Chartered and Robinhood executives in his X post.

First was the growing need for financial infrastructure that operates around the clock. Merrick noted that the next generation of digital asset markets will require always-on payment and settlement systems, rather than relying on traditional market opening hours. The second point was about the importance of bridging traditional finance (TradFi) and decentralized finance (DeFi). Merrick said that to achieve growth in tokenized markets, institutions will need bank-grade infrastructure, reliable custody solutions and effective risk management systems to participate at scale.

"Bridging TradFi & DeFi: Scaling tokenized markets requires real bank-grade infrastructure, custody, and risk management," Merrick wrote.

#5306. Hong Kong Passes Its Crypto Tax Reporting Law: Exchanges Must Collect User Data From 2027 and Share It Abroad From 2028

All reviews, research, news and assessments of any kind on The Tokenist are compiled using a strict editorial review process by our editorial team. Neither our writers nor our editors receive direct compensation of any kind to publish information on tokenist.com. Our company, Tokenist Media LLC, is community supported and may receive a small commission when you purchase products or services through links on our website. Click here for a full list of our partners and an in-depth explanation on how we get paid.

Hong Kong lawmakers passed a crypto tax reporting law on Wednesday, November 4, requiring crypto platforms tied to the city to collect their users’ tax details from 2027, so tax officials can share them with other countries from 2028.

The law brings in the OECD’s Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework, or CARF, the global standard for tracing crypto gains across borders. The government said Hong Kong’s Inland Revenue Department will start exchanging the data with partner jurisdictions in 2028.

The same bill updates the Common Reporting Standard, the system banks already use to report foreign accounts. Its new version, which also covers digital financial products, takes effect in 2028.

Hong Kong isn’t moving alone. It is one of 27 jurisdictions, including Singapore, the UAE and Switzerland, that have committed to first exchanges by 2028, the OECD’s latest list shows. Another 46, including the UK, the EU and Japan, start a year earlier.

So what does the new law ask of crypto platforms, and what changes for traders who use them?

It turns crypto platforms into tax reporters. The Inland Revenue Department’s CARF guide calls them reporting crypto-asset service providers: any business that carries out crypto trades for customers, whether as an exchange, a broker, a dealer or a crypto ATM operator.

A platform falls under Hong Kong’s rules if it is tax resident in the city, incorporated there, managed from there, or runs a branch or regular place of business there. Every platform that meets one of those tests has to register with the department, even if it has nothing to report.

Existing customers aren’t exempt. Platforms get 12 months after the rules take effect to collect self-certifications from users who already have accounts.

The law also sets offences for failing to register, skipping due diligence or filing wrong returns. Users can be prosecuted too, for knowingly or recklessly giving false information in a self-certification.

“Hong Kong has been supporting international efforts in enhancing tax transparency and combatting cross-border tax evasion,” said Christopher Hui, Hong Kong’s Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury.

Discover: Franklin Templeton Readies Two ETFs That Turn Stock Dividends Into Bitcoin as Washington Writes Crypto Rules Without Congress

On January 1, 2027, less than two months away. The bill moved quickly: a public consultation ran from December 2025 to February 2026, and the government published the bill on May 22.

Platforms that first fall under the rules in 2027 have until January 31, 2028, to register. The department hasn’t yet published the details of its online portal or the data format it wants.

Hong Kong is in the second wave. The OECD’s commitments list, last updated on September 14, splits the world like this:

Hong Kong’s rivals for crypto business are on the same schedule. Singapore and the UAE have also committed to their first exchanges by 2028.

Existing users will get the same request within a year. Lying on it is an offence under the new law, so ticking the wrong country isn’t a way around it.

That is usually enough for a tax office to spot crypto gains that never showed up on a return. Transfers to outside wallets are covered too, so moving coins off the exchange still leaves a record.

Platforms carry the heavier load. They have under two months to build the forms, the checks and the records, and the department has yet to publish its portal details.

For traders, Hong Kong’s crypto tax law closes one of the last big Asian gaps in the OECD’s reporting net. By 2028, a crypto account in Hong Kong, Singapore or Dubai will be about as visible to a home tax office as a bank account.

Apple has officially blocked the launch of tokenized trading in its shares on the new American platform OKXICE TSV. Exercising its thirty-day veto right under the SEC's "innovation exception," the iPhone manufacturer supported a large-scale demarche by issuers.

By November 2026, the number of boycotting companies had reached 59, which effectively paralyzed the largest regulatory experiment on crossing Wall Street with the crypto market.

🚨NEW: Three more issuers have objected to @okx/@ICE_Markets tokenizing their shares, bringing the total to 59: Apple The Home Depot GE Vernova Six of the Magnificent Seven have now objected. Meta wasn’t on the original list.

The OKXICE TSV project — a joint venture between the crypto exchange OKX and Intercontinental Exchange, the owner of the NYSE — was preparing to launch round-the-clock on-chain trading through Uniswap v4 pools on the XLayer blockchain.

However, at the moment, the listing has been blocked by six of the seven members of the "Magnificent Seven" (all except Meta, which was not initially on the lists), as well as SpaceX, The Home Depot, GE Vernova, JPMorgan Chase and Goldman Sachs.

Insiders link this coordinated refusal to corporations' unwillingness to lose control over capital and to harsh behind-the-scenes pressure from the traditional exchange Nasdaq, which actively persuaded issuers to derail the initiative.

This internal boycott has exposed a deep regulatory gap: while the legal union of TradFi and DeFi on U.S. territory has been put on pause by the issuers themselves, international capital has long been trading digital analogs of U.S. securities outside the country.

By the end of 2026, when global Bitcoin ownership reached 4.5–6% of the planet's population, an autonomous blockchain liquidity had formed in offshore jurisdictions.

Corporate America, in the person of Apple, is defending its sovereignty in the home market, but the offshore market will not be stopped by this.

#5303. Vitalik Buterin Reveals What Crypto Exchanges Must Do To Survive

Moneycontrol sat down with Ethereum founder Vitalik Buterin for an exclusive conversation on cryptocurrency security following the high-profile Binance breach.

The interviewer asked what guidance he would offer the industry after the incident underscored how even the most advanced exchanges remain exposed to cyberattacks and thefts, particularly as artificial intelligence tools grow more sophisticated.

Buterin replied by first pointing to encouraging trends in the underlying technology before turning to the practical mindset now taking hold across the sector. “The good news is that smart contract hacks have gone down a huge amount. All of the big hacks that we’ve seen over the last one and a half years, they’re much more concentrated in the user interface layer and in centralized components,” he said.

He added that while incidents haven’t disappeared, the foundation of reliable systems keeps strengthening, and leading firms are adjusting their priorities accordingly. “What we’ve been seeing is more and more people are realizing that their main responsibility for the next two years is not to win but to survive. Everyone is kind of figuring out what the concept of bunker mode means for them,” Buterin observed.

The Ethereum creator added that Binance’s decision to develop its own smart-chain infrastructure offers a useful example of how on-chain contracts can provide stronger protections, a direction he expects more platforms to pursue in the months ahead.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

In the latest development, Binance continues recovering from the October 29, 2026, $6.3 billion hack, the largest in crypto history and attributed to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group. The exchange has replenished nearly all affected assets from its own reserves, resumed phased withdrawals, and frozen roughly $3 billion of the stolen funds.

Binance founder Changpeng Zhao addressed the breach in a recent X post, stating, “A hack of this scale means serious security failures occurred. No platform is unhackable, but that cannot be an excuse.”

He further noted that certain details remain embarrassing, described the intrusion as a prolonged campaign that targeted numerous employees and systems, and stressed that as a shareholder, he expects the company to stay transparent, accept responsibility, and deliver meaningful security upgrades.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

#5302. Circle's USDC Dominates Stablecoin Market With 79% Share of Transaction Volume

Circle revealed that USDC accounted for 79% of the transaction volume of all stablecoins in the third quarter of 2026.

According to CEO Jeremy Allaire, the CEO of Circle explained that USDC's market share of the transaction volume of all stablecoins increased significantly from 66% in the same period a year ago. The overall USDC on-chain transaction volume was $13.9 trillion, an increase of 49% year-on-year.

This shows the rapid adoption of USDC in payments, trading, and blockchain-based financial applications despite stiff competition in the stablecoin space.

Circle stated that the issuance and redemption volumes of USDC in the third quarter reached a new high. In total, $208 billion of USDC was issued and redeemed in Q3. This translates to an average daily amount of $2.3 billion. For the third quarter, Circle said that the average USDC in circulation was $73.3 billion, which was up 18% year-on-year. This information was part of Circle's Q3 highlights.

Apart from USDC itself, Circle emphasized the growth in other aspects of its infrastructure. Circle indicated that Arc Mainnet went live in the third quarter. Over 100 institutions and applications are already building on Arc. As of Oct. 30, 2026, assets on Arc totaled $1.5 billion, as stated by Circle.

Circle Payment Network, or CPN, was another part of Circle's infrastructure that witnessed rapid growth. The company indicated that CPN ended the third quarter with an annualized payment volume of $41.3 billion. This was 15.2 times higher than in the same period last year, based on activity over the last 30 days. Allaire explained that CPN's payment volume is now more than $58 billion.

Circle also revealed that USDC has now become the leading settlement asset in agentic/automated internet payments. Allaire disclosed that over 99% of agent payments on x402 are settled in USDC.

In the third quarter, Circle's total revenue and reserve income were $865 million, up 17% year-on-year. This figure included $182 million from ARC token sales, according to an image showing Circle's Q3 highlights.

According to Allaire, the impressive performance in the third quarter is a strong signal that Circle is ready for the next phase of stablecoin adoption. He said the GENIUS Act, which is expected to take effect in January, will bring regulated digital dollars into the mainstream. Also, Circle has now activated all the layers of its platform.

The impressive third-quarter data indicates that Circle has not only further solidified USDC's dominance in terms of transaction activity but is also expanding its ecosystem across payments, on-chain finance, and institutional adoption.

American Riot Platforms Inc. (RIOT) sold off 79% of its Bitcoin in the third quarter of 2026, redirecting capital toward building infrastructure for artificial intelligence. According to a fresh financial report, the company reduced its cryptocurrency reserves from 11,380 to 2,418 BTC.

In total, over the first nine months of the year, Riot sold 20,264 BTC on the market, receiving about $1.5 billion for them. This money went toward financing a major technological shift: the company's free energy capacity is being repurposed for high-performance computing needs.

Riot shares reacted to the session open with a sharp jump to $16.20, after which they stabilized in the $15.45–$15.50 range, holding positions on elevated volumes.

The main incentive for selling the cryptocurrency was a 15-year agreement to lease ready-made sites and capacities (powered land lease) totaling 910 MW at the Corsicana campus in Texas. The strategic partner was the Frontier AI Lab (Anthropic) laboratory.

The initial cost of the contract is estimated at $28 billion, and the average annual rent at the start will be about $1.8 billion. Taking into account other projects, Riot's total long-term revenue in the data center segment has reached $38 billion, and the total controlled capacity is 1,151 MW.

Riot CEO Jason Les noted that the agreement is structured as a triple-net lease. Under its terms, the client itself purchases and maintains the computing equipment. For Riot, this reduces construction costs by roughly half compared to standard Tier 3 data centers. As a result, the company will be able to do without issuing new shares and diluting investors' stakes.

The shift in focus is occurring against the backdrop of falling margins in classic mining. Riot's quarterly revenue from cryptocurrency mining fell by 28% — to $116 million, although the company actually mined 1,637 BTC.

Nevertheless, total quarterly revenue held at $181.4 million (+1% year-over-year), outpacing market forecasts. Net profit amounted to $4.03 million.

To optimize its balance sheet, the company fully closed its $200 million credit line with Coinbase, returning 5,821 BTC from collateral. Riot ended the quarter with free liquidity of $950.2 million (including cash and the remainder of the cryptocurrency). The balance sheet retains 2,418 BTC, which may also go under the hammer in the fourth quarter to finance the Texas construction.

#5299. XRP Ledger Activates New Amendment to Strengthen Network

The XRP Ledger (XRPL) network recently activated a new amendment that helps secure the network by resolving potential security weaknesses and making some existing functionalities more robust and reliable.

This latest amendment, called fixCleanup3_4_0, was activated on Nov. 4, bringing a series of technical updates that include fixes for token issuance, automated market makers (AMMs), lending functionalities, and other parts of the XRP Ledger network.

A fix for a potential security weak point related to token issuance on the XRP Ledger network is a critical aspect of the latest amendment.

As explained in the official documentation of the XRP Ledger network, this update addresses a potential weakness related to delegated permissions that could allow some accounts to issue tokens when they are only allowed to destroy them.

On the XRP Ledger, token issuers can grant permissions to other accounts to perform certain tasks. For example, a stablecoin issuer could delegate permission to burn tokens to another account when customers want to redeem them.

With the latest amendment, the XRP Ledger network addresses this security weakness by preventing a zero-balance, burn-only delegated payment from resulting in the issuance of new tokens.

On top of addressing token issuance permissions, there's more to the fixCleanup3_4_0 amendment.

As explained in the official XRP Ledger network documentation, the fixCleanup3_4_0 update brings several fixes to decentralized trading, asset management, and transaction processing.

For automated market makers (AMMs), this latest update prevents some invalid auction bids and makes some improvements to how liquidity withdrawals and token clawbacks work.

It also brings some fixes for potential unexpected calculation errors or rounding issues that could occur in some cases.

These changes are supposed to make things more predictable when it comes to liquidity pools and avoid potential failures that could happen in some cases.

Another significant aspect of these changes concerns Single Asset Vaults and the proposed native lending infrastructure on the XRP Ledger.

As explained, this amendment brings some improvements to how rounding is handled when assets enter or exit vaults.

The idea is to ensure that transactions do not result in more or fewer assets being transferred than they should.

#5298. Ripple Executive Reveals Massive Growth of Company's London Hub

According to Ripple's UK and Europe Managing Director, Cassie Craddock, Ripple’s London office has expanded significantly over the last decade to become Ripple’s largest international hub outside the U.S.

“When we moved into our current office in 2018, there were 2 floors, and a lot of empty desks. Now we’re on 3 floors and full on all the desks. We’re now over capacity,” she wrote on X.

Craddock's comments came after she took part in a fireside chat at the British Residence in New York as part of Ripple’s Swell conference.

She revealed that Ripple chose to focus on London early on, given the UK's strong capital markets, mature legal system, experienced regulators and concentration of financial talent.

However, she added that regulatory uncertainty had previously limited the company’s capacity to build more relationships with leading U.K. financial institutions.

Ripple's story in the U.K. capital began on March 21, 2016, when the San Francisco-based company officially announced the launch of its first office in London, located in Canary Wharf.

Back then, the expansion was meant to accommodate the growing interest of European banks in distributed ledger technology and cross-border settlement solutions.

Ripple incorporated its U.K. entity in April 2016 under the name Ripple Europe Ltd. (later changed to Ripple Markets UK Ltd. in August 2022).

Ripple continued to expand its ties to U.K. financial institutions in the following years.

In April 2018, Santander introduced its new international payments app, One Pay FX, which used Ripple’s xCurrent technology.

In February 2022, Ripple announced a partnership with London-based payments company Modulr to make it easier to send cross-border payments to the UK and Europe.

Moreover, Ripple has played a role in developing the research landscape for blockchain in the U.K. In January 2026, Ripple shared that it had pledged more than £5M to UK universities under its University Blockchain Research Initiative.

One of the major milestones for Ripple in the U.K. occurred on Jan. 9, when Ripple received an Electronic Money Institution license and cryptoasset registration from the Financial Conduct Authority. The authorizations enabled Ripple to extend its regulated cross-border payment services to UK institutions.

In February, Ripple also secured a partnership with Aviva Investors to explore the tokenization of traditional investment funds.

This work resulted in the launch of a tokenized share class of Aviva Investors’ £22bn Sterling Liquidity Fund on the XRP Ledger on Oct. 26.

#5296. Bitcoin Miner and Whale Signals Spike on Binance: CryptoQuant Lays Out a Three-Part Test for a New Rally, and BTC Has Passed One

All reviews, research, news and assessments of any kind on The Tokenist are compiled using a strict editorial review process by our editorial team. Neither our writers nor our editors receive direct compensation of any kind to publish information on tokenist.com. Our company, Tokenist Media LLC, is community supported and may receive a small commission when you purchase products or services through links on our website. Bitcoin miners and whales sent unusually large amounts of BTC toward exchanges in recent days, CryptoQuant said on Thursday, November 5, and its analyst argues the spikes could be early signs of a new rally if three conditions are met.

That sounds backwards at first. Coins heading to exchanges usually mean someone wants to sell.

Bitcoin: Miner and Whale Indicators Surge—Early Signs of a New Rally?“Continued MPI normalization, absorption of large deposits, and a recovery above those highs supported by spot volume would strengthen the case that a new rally is beginning.” – By COINDREAM pic.twitter.com/z8D5EBBdvC

On Binance, the exchange whale ratio, the share of inflows coming from the 10 largest deposits, jumped to near 1.0, above its February–March peaks of about 0.85–0.87. The Miners’ Position Index (MPI), which compares miners’ outflows with their yearly average, spiked to about 2.9 before falling back to about 0.2.

The spikes came around the US midterms, when BTC dropped to $75,736 on election night and then bounced back above $80,000. It traded at $80,120 on Binance at 11:10 UTC on Thursday.

So were whales and miners selling into the bounce, or was the market strong enough to take their coins?

A few big wallets and Bitcoin miners moved a lot of coins at once, and the price rose anyway. That is the part CryptoQuant analyst COINDREAM finds interesting.

The whale ratio’s reading near 1.0 means almost all of the BTC arriving at Binance came in the 10 largest transfers. CryptoQuant’s chart puts it above the February and March peaks.

The miner signal has a mixed record. The MPI spiked during February’s sell-off and again during August’s rebound, so the spike alone does not say which way the price goes next. What follows it matters more.

Miners had a reason to move coins. Bitcoin’s mining difficulty rose 5.5% on October 29, the same day BTC fell on news of the Binance hack, so each unit of computing power earned less just as the price dropped. With hashrate near 1,030 EH/s, mempool.space estimates the next adjustment on November 13 will cut difficulty by about 2.8%.

One caveat: neither metric proves a sale. CryptoQuant’s own chart notes that miner outflows are not the same as confirmed selling.

The analyst set out what would turn the signal bullish: “Continued MPI normalization, absorption of large deposits, and a recovery above those highs supported by spot volume would strengthen the case that a new rally is beginning.”

Discover: Bitcoin Sits on Its 200-Day Average as Democrats Close In on Both Chambers of Congress: Is the Crypto Market Structure Bill Out of Time?

One is met, one is holding for now, and one is not there yet.

Miner pressure: met. The MPI is back to about 0.2 after its spike, close to normal.

Absorbing big deposits: so far, yes. BTC rose 3.9% on Wednesday to close at $80,504, even with the whale deposits sitting on Binance. Buyers took 54% of Binance spot trading that day. Thursday looks weaker: sellers have led with 61% of trades so far, and the price has slipped back to about $80,120.

A move above the highs on spot volume: not yet. The nearest high is $81,971, where BTC traded on October 29 before the Binance hack news broke. Binance spot volume hit $1.75 billion on Wednesday, 52% above its 30-day average of $1.15 billion, but still below the $1.91 billion traded on the day of the hack.

That last condition is the one to watch. Without strong spot buying above $81,971, the whale and miner spikes could just as easily be selling that the market happened to absorb.

Discover: Binance Says Its $6.3 Billion Hack Began With a Fake Job Interview, but Traders Aren’t Convinced

BTC is sitting right on its moving averages. The 20-day EMA is at $79,965 and the 50-day EMA at $80,149, so the $80,000 area is the first support.

The advance case lines up with CryptoQuant’s third condition. A close above $81,971 would put Bitcoin back where it was before the hack, and strong spot volume would show real buyers are behind the move.

#5295. Yield-Bearing eZAR Blurs the Line Between Stablecoin and Investment Product

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

eZAR opened its rand-pegged token to the public on November 2 with R303 million in circulation. Its reserve yield is the feature that puts the stablecoin label to the test.

Most stablecoin launches promise a token that never moves. eZAR's disclosures say its holders can make money or lose it. The rand-pegged token went live to the public on November 2, and its fine print reads more like an investment product than a payments coin.

According to launch reports, eZAR is now open to the public and to new institutional partners after almost a year of pilot operations. The company says R303 million worth of tokens had been issued and were in circulation as of October 30.

The project is a partnership between eZAR Ltd, asset manager Ninety One and AVBOB Financial Services, with AVBOB acting as lead institution and liquidity partner. CEO Sean Emery said the team put "getting it right" ahead of "getting it big" during the pilot. The message now is that eZAR is ready to scale.

The model also departs from the typical single-issuer coin. Neobanks, retailers, insurers and payment firms can plug the token into their own branded wallets and share in the economics. Transfers between participating wallets settle within seconds at any hour and, according to the company, cost nothing.

The reserves backing eZAR are invested through a money market strategy run by Ninety One, mainly in the Ninety One Money Market Fund. Returns are distributed daily to partners after partnership fees, and each partner then decides on what terms its own customers receive a share.

Ninety One's head of digital assets, Adam Duxbury, described it as new rails under an old discipline. His firm has run money market strategies for 25 years, he said, and South Africa should build its own digital rand rather than import a dollar coin.

The framing is clever, since it presents the yield as a feature of "digital cash that can grow." Yet that same feature makes the classification question hard to avoid.

The risk language is the most revealing part of the launch. eZAR describes itself as a crypto asset issued by the eZAR En Commandite Partnership. It states that the token is not legal tender, not a bank deposit and not a banking product, and that it carries no guarantee.

The details that follow set it further apart. The R1 redemption value depends on available liquidity. Money market returns can be positive or negative, so capital is at risk. Holders also own no units in the underlying fund and have no direct claim on it.

"Capital at risk" rarely appears in stablecoin terms. A payments token is meant to hold its value and let users redeem at par, yet eZAR's own documents hedge on both counts. Back in March, a market survey from Blockhouse had already noted that eZAR doesn't qualify as a stablecoin under most regulations. The live launch now tests that observation against a real product.

In the major rulebooks, the yield is the sticking point. The US GENIUS Act bars permitted payment stablecoin issuers from paying holders any form of interest or yield solely for holding, using or retaining the token. The EU's MiCA framework takes a similar line on interest. The logic is that a payment token paying a return starts to function like an unregulated deposit.

The OCC issued its final GENIUS Act rules on October 21, and they confirmed that ban for covered issuers. The contested ground lies elsewhere, in who sits between the issuer and the holder. Earlier OCC proposals set a rebuttable presumption against yield arrangements run through affiliates and related third parties, whereas the statute itself names only issuers.

eZAR's design lands squarely in that gray zone. Returns flow to partners, and the partners decide how customers share in them. Whether that amounts to an issuer paying yield or a partner passing on profit is precisely the kind of question US regulators are now wrestling with, and it would be a difficult one to argue before the OCC.

eZAR doesn't operate under the US or EU regimes, so none of those rules apply to it directly. eZAR Ltd is described as an authorised financial services provider responsible for the main technology and services behind the partnership. That technology also draws on the South African Reserve Bank's Project Khokha 2, where eZAR's parent company, Block Markets Africa, was a technical contributor.

This background signals a serious, institution-backed build rather than a speculative launch. Even so, the rand stablecoin field is getting crowded. ZARU launched earlier this year as an institutional-grade rand coin, and a pattern is emerging of different models competing for the same local payments niche.

The bigger question is whether South Africa will define stablecoins narrowly, as the US and EU do, or leave room for hybrid products like this one. Because the network is permissioned, the reported circulation figure also rests on company disclosure rather than a public ledger, which makes the regulatory and disclosure framework matter even more.

For everyday users, the appeal is easy to see. A rand token that moves in seconds, costs nothing to send and might earn a daily return makes an attractive pitch. For partners, shared infrastructure with a revenue share offers a way into digital payments without building a coin from scratch.

The trade-off sits in the disclaimers. A holder who treats eZAR like a bank balance could be caught off guard by liquidity-dependent redemption, or by a money market return that dips below zero. That gap between how the product feels and how it is legally defined is where regulators tend to step in.

eZAR is best understood as a hybrid: a payments token with an investment return attached. It may well succeed on those terms. Still, as more jurisdictions tighten the stablecoin definition around no-yield, par-redemption tokens, products like this will increasingly be judged on what they are rather than what they are called. How South African regulators treat eZAR in the coming months will show which way that debate is heading.

#5294. Binance's CZ Sounds Alarm Over New Crypto Phishing Scam

Binance co-founder Changpeng Zhao (CZ) has warned about a malicious crypto phishing scheme that uses a fake Trust Wallet website to lure unsuspecting users into connecting their wallets.

CZ shared a warning about a fraudulent website with a fake domain that mimics the popular Trust Wallet website.

Attackers modified the website domain by replacing the “u” with “a” and changing the extension from “.com” to “.cam,” which may trick unsuspecting users who don’t carefully inspect the domain.

The malicious website tricks users into connecting their crypto wallets in order to review their transfers.

However, the site contains JavaScript code that attempts to scan wallet balances using a backend API in order to prepare transfers to specific wallet addresses.

The attacker’s setup works with multiple well-known crypto wallets such as Trust Wallet, Phantom, and OKX Wallet.

CZ’s warning comes shortly after a surge in crypto phishing attempts against wallet users.

On Nov. 3, cybersecurity firm Bitdefender announced that scammers had started using the recent Binance security breach to spread fake emails impersonating Trust Wallet.

The phishing emails suggested that Trust Wallet users were also impacted by the Binance security breach. Therefore, they instructed users to perform a mandatory wallet verification procedure.

The email messages warned that users would be suspended after Nov. 7 if they did not complete the wallet verification process.

Bitdefender said that the phishing scheme affected users in multiple countries, including the United States, United Kingdom, Australia, Ireland and South Africa.

The phishing messages led users to fake verification websites where their wallet credentials or recovery data could be leaked.

Earlier this year, cybersecurity analysts from CYFIRMA spotted another phishing attack against Trust Wallet users. The attackers used malicious QR codes on Telegram to target Trust Wallet users.

#5293. Wall Street Power Grab? Anti-Crypto Elizabeth Warren Could Put Day Trading in the Crosshairs

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Elizabeth Warren is preparing to take control of the Senate Banking Committee, putting one of Washington’s most outspoken financial regulators at the center of America’s next market policy battle. Her expected appointment could bring renewed scrutiny to Wall Street, crypto, and the rules governing retail day trading.

With Democrats taking control of both chambers of Congress in the November 2026 midterms, Warren will have a stronger platform to investigate financial firms and challenge federal regulators. Her priorities could extend beyond traditional banking, bringing day trading platforms, market structure, and prediction markets into the congressional red-list.

JUST IN: 🇺🇸 Anti-crypto Senator Elizabeth Warren expected to become Chair of Senate Banking Committee, giving her major power over the financial industry. pic.twitter.com/t2nvMSdo1U

The Massachusetts senator has spent years arguing that financial markets need stronger protections for ordinary Americans. Now, she could have the committee authority to turn those arguments into hearings, investigations, and legislative proposals.

The connection to day trading is not simply about whether Americans can buy and sell stocks freely. It is about the market infrastructure that determines how retail orders are executed, priced, and routed.

Elizabeth Warren has already taken a position on one important part of that debate. On October 1, she joined four Democratic senators in urging SEC Chairman Paul Atkins to preserve key Regulation National Market System protections.

The lawmakers opposed proposed changes to Rules 611 and 610(e), warning that removing protections could allow retail orders to execute at worse prices. They argued that larger market participants could benefit while ordinary investors faced higher trading costs.

For day trading platforms and their customers, these rules matter. Fast-moving traders depend on competitive execution, transparent pricing and reliable access to market liquidity.

Warren’s intervention shows that retail trading infrastructure is already on her regulatory agenda. Her committee leadership could give her more opportunities to question the SEC about how brokers, exchanges and market makers handle individual investors’ orders.

This does not mean Warren has proposed restrictions on day trading itself. There is currently no confirmed proposal from her to limit how frequently retail investors can trade.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Day trading is only one potential part of Warren’s expanding financial oversight agenda. The senator has also raised concerns about prediction markets, particularly the possibility of insider trading involving contracts tied to political and economic events.

The Wall Street Journal reported that Warren intends to examine alleged insider trading in prediction markets alongside private equity, major banks and crypto companies. Meanwhile, Democrats are preparing investigations into financial relationships between the crypto industry, Trump and his family.

Warren is expected to lead the Senate Banking Committee and has pledged to examine alleged deals connecting the industry with the president.

Senator Elizabeth Warren accuses President Donald Trump of using his presidency to benefit wealthy donors and corporate allies at the expense of ordinary Americans. In a video posted on X, Warren points to corporate donations, dropped lawsuits, cryptocurrency ventures and airline… pic.twitter.com/bQ1twXJfvN

Those investigations could put companies with political and financial connections under greater pressure. They could also consume congressional attention that the crypto industry had hoped to devote to market structure legislation.

On day trading businesses, the consequences may be less direct but still important. Congressional scrutiny of retail trading protections, prediction markets, and financial intermediaries could influence how regulators approach trading platforms.

Warren’s critics may argue that additional regulation risks increasing compliance costs and limiting competition. Her supporters, meanwhile, point to investor protections and fair market access as reasons for stronger oversight.

The bigger question is how far Elizabeth Warren intends to take that agenda once she assumes the committee chairmanship. With subpoena powers, control over hearings, and a stronger legislative platform, she will have more influence over the financial industry’s relationship with federal regulators.

#5290. Polygon Plans Hard Fork to Seize $6.5 Million From Polymarket and Binance Hackers

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

Polygon developers now propose a step that has long been considered an absolute taboo in the crypto industry. They put to a vote a plan to rescue Binance and Polymarket money, and this plan is, to say it mildly, radical — zero out the hackers’ wallets at the protocol level. Ongoing cybersecurity crisis shows no signs of stopping, and now the industry is being faced with an uncomfortable choice: save systemic players or protect the inviolability of Web3’s main rule that transactions cannot be reversed. The Polygon PoS hard fork involves seizing 70.49 million POL tokens ($6.5 million at the time of the attack) from the hacker addresses to return them to the victims.

The crisis unfolded at the end of October after two independent hacks. The stolen assets were scattered across five wallets (23.86 million POL was taken from Polymarket, 46.63 million from Binance). Yes, Polygon validators immediately blacklisted the addresses, cutting off the outflow, but this is just an attempt to hold back the dam with bare hands. Manual blocking is a temporary plug, and the authors of the proposal openly admit it.

The hacker is not giving up either and is continuously bombarding the network with transactions carrying wild fees of up to 219,000 POL, counting on automation or a validator with a weakness for easy money to let the operation through for a windfall profit. Things have gone as far as direct attempts to bribe validators with cash, and the hacker simply ignored on-chain negotiations. The developers’ logic is simple: keeping millions in a manual “ban” forever is a dead end that leaves the entire network under constant fire.

No one has access to the hacker’s private keys, so Polygon is changing the consensus rules themselves. Should the hard fork get approval at a certain block, the hackers’ balances will be zeroed out, and an equivalent amount will be mirror-credited to verified Binance and Polymarket wallets — without any token printing.

Polygon Labs is well aware that such an administrative step completely negates the very idea of decentralization.

This plan inevitably triggers a strong sense of the notorious The DAO hard fork of 2016. Back then, to save the young Ethereum ecosystem, developers also had to go through a painful split of the community and ignore the “Code is Law” principle. But Polygon Labs hopes that in their case consensus among validators is already rock-solid, so they are narrowing the framework of the precedent as much as possible, positioning the fork as an exclusively one-time action.

The fate of the millions in POL token is being decided right now in a community vote. The largest validators are already in favor, since both platforms are critically important to Polygon’s survival. If the plan is approved, the software will be released after two weeks of testing, and exchanges and node operators will have to urgently update. Those who refuse to switch to the new code face automatic isolation on the old branch of the blockchain — with no connection to the main network.

#5289. Canton Coin Gets SEC "Digital Commodity" Label: Here's What the Two Prongs Actually Mean

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The SEC's Division of Corporation Finance called Canton Coin a digital commodity on November 3. The ruling rests on two representations, including the absence of a "central party."

The most important words in the SEC's Canton Coin letter aren't "digital commodity." They are the ones the staff put in front of that label: the conclusion holds "in reliance on the representations" Canton's lawyers made. The SEC didn't independently prove the network has no central party. It accepted a description and attached a conclusion to it.

On November 3, the Division of Corporation Finance's Office of Chief Counsel answered Canton Network's October 30 request. The response came from Deputy Chief Counsel Jonathan A. Ingram and was addressed to the staff team of Ted Yu, Andrew Schoeffler and Mark Vilardo. The Division said it views Canton Coin as a "digital commodity" as the term is described in the SEC's March interpretation.

It also said it will not recommend enforcement action if Canton Coin is minted programmatically by Super Validators, Validators and application providers, as described in the request. That holds without registration under Section 5 of the Securities Act or Section 12(g) of the Exchange Act, and it applies if the issuer relies on an opinion of counsel. The facts the staff relied on are laid out in the Canton Network's incoming letter.

Early coverage focused on the classification label. The more useful story, though, is how the staff got there.

The staff pointed to two representations. The first is that Canton Coin is intrinsically linked to, and derives its value from, the programmatic operation of the Canton Network, along with supply and demand dynamics. Its value does not come from an expectation of profits from the essential managerial efforts of others.

That phrase echoes the Howey test, the long-standing U.S. framework for investment contracts. The prong asks a simple question: when someone holds this token, are they betting on a team's work, or on a network that runs by itself? On the facts presented, the staff's answer was the network.

This is the more familiar half of the analysis, and most token projects argue some version of it. Because almost every issuer makes the same claim, the first prong carries less weight on its own, which is why the second one deserves a closer look.

The second representation is that the Canton Network has no "central party," as the March interpretation defines that term. In the SEC and CFTC's framework, a digital commodity belongs to a functional crypto system that has no central party overseeing participation or distributing rewards to users.

This prong is the one to watch, because Canton Coin is minted by Super Validators, Validators and application providers. Those are named roles in a structured network, so a skeptic could fairly ask whether the Super Validator tier looks like a central party in practice. The letter's answer rests on the word "programmatically": the minting follows protocol rules rather than anyone's discretion.

Legal commentators reading the March interpretation have also pointed out that it doesn't fully explain how the "central party" concept relates to its separate definition of decentralization. The Canton letter doesn't settle that either. It applies the term to one set of facts and stops there.

A no-action letter is narrower than it sounds. The Division itself says the response states its position on enforcement action only and expresses no legal conclusion on the issues presented. It also says the positions rest on the representations in the request, and that different facts or conditions might lead to different conclusions.

In practice, that comes down to three points. First, the letter is staff-level guidance rather than a Commission vote. Second, it protects reliance on the specific arrangement described, not the token in every future circumstance. Third, if the representations change, the comfort can disappear.

For a company, the letter is still valuable, since a written statement that staff won't recommend enforcement is a strong signal. Even so, it shouldn't be mistaken for a permanent legal classification. It is a snapshot of staff views based on facts someone else supplied.

The framework behind the letter is the Commission's March 17 interpretation, which the CFTC joined. It sorts crypto assets into five categories: digital commodities, digital collectibles, digital tools, stablecoins and digital securities. Four of the five are generally treated as non-securities, and the securities analysis stays fact-specific for the rest.

The two documents do different jobs. The interpretation is a general map: it tells the market how the Commission thinks about categories and which features push an asset one way or the other. The Canton letter is an application. It takes a named token, tests it against the map's digital commodity category, and gives a case-specific enforcement answer.

That sequence matters. The interpretation says what a digital commodity looks like, and the letter says that, if the facts are as represented, Canton Coin looks like one.

The practical lesson is about preparation. Canton's request framed its facts to fit the two prongs, and the staff responded in those terms. Projects hoping for similar treatment will likely follow the same template: document how value arises from network operation, and document why no single party oversees participation or distributes rewards.

The harder test will come from tokens with more visible governance or a more active operating team. Those projects will have to explain why their structure doesn't amount to a central party, and the Canton letter doesn't say where that line sits.

For now, the letter works best as an early data point rather than a final answer. The classification label drew the attention, but the representations behind it are what other projects will study. How the staff handles the next request, especially one with a messier governance story, will show whether the "no central party" prong is a narrow gate or a wide one.

#5287. South Korea Announces Delay in Crypto Taxation Policy

South Korea announced a delay in the introduction of its cryptocurrency capital gains tax until 2029, extending the tax-free period by two years as authorities plan on strengthening regulatory oversight and connecting data from exchanges with the United States, yna.co.kr reports.

Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il announced the proposal Thursday, acknowledging that the government would be postponing the controversial tax for a fourth time already.

Originally, the policy was scheduled to become active in January 2022: it would impose a 22% tax, local income tax on all cryptocurrency-related gains that exceed 2.5 million won.

While the proposed delay could provide a relief for the South Korean cryptocurrency market and even support the domestic trading activity, it remains a substantial risk factor for both local and overseas investors.

Officials argue that implementing the tax before international information-sharing systems become operational could disadvantage local exchanges and complicate enforcement against overseas trading activity.

Future tax liabilities aren't going to be eliminated, additional time to develop a comprehensive taxation network is more likely to enforce even more limitations on investors in the future, rather than a premature implementation with various legal loopholes.

The government also intends to introduce provisions allowing investors to carry forward cryptocurrency investment losses for up to three years, potentially reducing taxable gains in subsequent periods.

South Korea is also going to establish a separate working group that is going to further refine taxation rules and hopefully simplify reporting requirements for investors, considering the complexity of reporting digital assets transactions and traders on exchanges.

Legislative amendments are expected to reach the National Assembly in 2027.

Authorities reported the continuous coordinating with the Financial Services Commission to accelerate digital assets legislation, providing more transparency and investors protection.

For the industry in general, the proposed extension is more of a transition stage that should improve the competitiveness of the digital assets market, despite introducing stricter tax enforcement. Unfortunately for retail investors, it creates another barrier that might push fresh funds further away from the industry.

It's worth noting that platforms like Galaxy Digital and Copper offer different services, including trading and custody, for institutional clients.

It's worth mentioning that the latest BTC movements come after a few similar transactions involving MARA throughout October.

On Oct. 9, MARA moved around 996 BTC ($81.13 million at that time) to a wallet linked to crypto platform Galaxy Digital.

The transaction prompted some speculation about possible BTC selling, though it didn't confirm whether Galaxy Digital actually liquidated the assets or not.

On Oct. 19, Lookonchain again identified some other transactions involving wallets linked to the Bitcoin miner.

As per the analytics firm's data, the wallets linked to the Bitcoin miner sent 1,000 BTC (approximately $82.8 million) to crypto exchanges like Binance.

Towards the end of October, concerns over possible selling increased.

#5285. South Korea Delays Its Crypto Tax to 2029, a Fourth Postponement That Still Needs Lawmakers’ Approval

All reviews, research, news and assessments of any kind on The Tokenist are compiled using a strict editorial review process by our editorial team. Neither our writers nor our editors receive direct compensation of any kind to publish information on tokenist.com. Our company, Tokenist Media LLC, is community supported and may receive a small commission when you purchase products or services through links on our website. Click here for a full list of our partners and an in-depth explanation on how we get paid.

South Korea’s government will push its 22% crypto tax back two years to 2029, Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il said on Thursday, November 5, a day after Democratic Party leader Kim Min-seok asked for the delay.

Korean traders have now heard “not yet” four times.

The levy would charge 22%, a 20% national rate plus 2% local tax, on yearly gains from virtual assets above ₩2.5 million, about $1,860. It was due to start in January 2027. Lee announced the plan at an emergency briefing at the Government Complex Seoul, saying the ministry will consult with the National Assembly on a two-year deferral.

It is a quick turn. As recently as the summer, the government had confirmed the tax would go ahead in January 2027, with no new delay in its yearly tax plan.

So why does Seoul keep moving the date, and did Korea’s crypto market even notice?

The official reason this time is data. Tax information exchange with the US on crypto accounts starts in 2029, and the ministry says taxing earlier would leave users of local exchanges worse off than traders on offshore platforms the tax office can’t yet see.

Lee gave three reasons in all. Besides the US exchange, he named the need to refine the rules, including deductions for carried-over losses, and the trading and regulatory changes coming with Korea’s digital asset act.

The loss rule matters most for traders. Under the current law, gains and losses are counted one year at a time. The government now wants losses carried forward for up to three years and deducted from later gains, pointing to how far crypto prices swing.

Politics did the rest. Seoul Economic Daily wrote that the deciding factor was fading support among young adults, who make up most of Korea’s crypto investors, and both the ruling and opposition parties had called for another delay.

Lee said he takes it “seriously” that he is announcing another deferral after three earlier ones.

The tax was written into law in 2020 and first set for January 2022. Lawmakers moved it to 2023 in December 2021, to 2025 in December 2022, and to 2027 in December 2024.

The new plan has its own schedule. A public-private working group will join international talks on sharing crypto tax data, rule changes come in the first half of 2027, amendments go to the National Assembly’s regular session that year, and detailed tax standards follow in the first half of 2028.

One caveat: none of this is law yet. The statute still says January 2027 until lawmakers pass an amendment, though the request came from the ruling party’s own leader.

For now, very little changes. Gains stay untaxed for two more years if the amendment passes, and the market barely moved on the news.

Upbit’s KRW markets traded ₩1.36 trillion, about $1.01 billion, in the 24 hours to 14:33 UTC on Thursday. XRP led with ₩146.7 billion, or 10.8% of the total, ahead of Bitcoin’s ₩114.3 billion.

Korean prices are almost level with global ones. Bitcoin cost ₩107.05 million on Upbit, about $79,570 at ₩1,345 per dollar, just 0.1% above Binance. That gap, the “kimchi premium”, tends to widen when local demand runs hot.

XRP, Upbit’s most traded coin, sits at $1.30 on Binance, down 14% in 30 days. It trades below the 50-day EMA at $1.3348 and the 200-day EMA at $1.3628, with resistance at $1.3444 and support at $1.2562. Below that, the next swing low is $1.2002.

Korea’s traders get another two years without a bill. Whether 2029 sticks depends on the same lawmakers who moved the date three times before.

#5284. Binance Revokes API Keys, Security Issue Found at SignalPlus

Binance has revoked all API keys associated with SignalPlus after the digital asset trading infrastructure provider identified a potential security vulnerability, prompting the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange to take measures to protect users, according to the latest report on the Binance's official Square feed.

The exchange confirmed Thursday that the decision was intended to prevent possible unauthorized access through connections established between Binance accounts and SignalPlus. Binance emphasized that its internal systems had not been compromised and that customer funds remained safe.

For now, the reason or the nature of the incident remains unclear. Both companies have yet to disclose how serious the potential vulnerability is or how many users may be affected. It is still unclear whether the attackers gained access to customer accounts or if the incident caused any financial losses.

The development underscores the security challenges associated with third-party infrastructure in cryptocurrency markets, where trading platforms increasingly depend on external applications for execution, analytics and automation.

Binance's security documentation advises users to revoke potentially compromised credentials immediately and restrict API permissions to necessary functions.

For affected SignalPlus users, restoring automated trading functionality may require generating new credentials once the integration is deemed secure.

SignalPlus provides trading infrastructure and analytical tools for cryptocurrency derivatives markets, allowing traders to manage positions and execute strategies across exchanges through API integrations.

These connections enable third-party applications to interact with exchange accounts without requiring users to transfer their assets off-platform. However, depending on the permissions granted, compromised API credentials can potentially expose accounts to unauthorized trading activity.

Binance has effectively severed existing integrations between its platform and SignalPlus. The measure could potentially disrupt automated trading strategies that rely on those connections.

According to one of the architects of the XRP Ledger, now Ripple CTO Emeritus David Schwartz, his retirement from active development almost a year ago came at the right time. "I picked a great time to retire!", said Schwartz, reacting to the latest report from OpenAI researchers, which touches on testing a new cyber model. Just one autonomous run and the AI completely changed the familiar standards of network security, OpenAI researcher Eric Wallace confirms.

The report shows how OpenAI's pipeline works. First thing to understand, it's a fully complete cycle: the system independently finds a potential bug, verifies it, writes a working exploit to confirm it and automatically releases a patch. This was tested on the Linux kernel, the core software that runs most of the planet's servers (including OpenAI's own compute clusters).

The Web3 sphere is one where open-source code is the foundation of blockchain security, so this development is a challenge to say the least. If AI finds zero-day vulnerabilities in a matter of hours, manual code auditing by humans becomes useless.

Yes, Schwartz stepped down from the post of Ripple CTO into honorary retirement last November, but he hasn't abandoned his terminal. Just recently he showed monitoring charts of his personal server hub on the XRP Ledger network. There, a node is running under colossal load: it maintains more than 550 active connections (peers), shows latency of around 200ms and processes about 110,000 incoming messages per second.

Besides, Schwartz continues personal work on the network's internal architectural problems. In a discussion with active validators, Schwartz detailed a transaction queue bug that caused the local load metric on his server to jump to 540, triggering fee spikes within the ledger.

Schwartz picked the "right time" to step back from Ripple, but he's clearly not out of the game.
